Innate Immune Response - Neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells, mast cells, eosinophils, basophils.  Adaptive Immune Response - Dendritic Cells (which bridge the gap), T & B cells. Dendritic Cells have PRRs (Pattern Recognition Receptors) on their surface which allow them to detect the presence of PAMPs (Pathogen Associated Molecular Patterns). They then travel from the site of detection to the closest draining lymph node where they present the antigen to naïve T & B cells. Naïve T & B cells recognise the antigen presented by the DC due to their specific receptors, become activated and proliferate. Once activated they differentiate into effector cells and travel back to the site of infection where they perform their effector function. This process is known as Primary Response. After this, if there is still infection present, the same process occurs, however the crossover of T & B cells is enhanced. T & B cells now don't need to interact with a dendritic cell, instead they can directly recognise the antigen and become activated. This process is called Memory Response and means that if the pathogen returns, these pre-made effector cells are already present and ready to fight the infection. We don’t need to go through primary response again. The correct answer is C  Type 1 respiratory failure is oxygenation failure. Symptoms include low PiO2 and high Pco2. It is caused by a pulmonary shunt which is a ventilation perfusion ratio of <0.5. This means that there is insufficient time for the alveoli to be fully ventilated and in turn they do not get filled with all of the air. As a result the blood supplying these alveoli does not contain enough O2. The symptoms of this may be treated with oxygen therapy however it will not cure the condition as the problem lies within the lungs itself. The best way to treat this is to identify and treat the cause of the shunt. This could be due to a pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism or heart failure.  B- VQ Mismatch is actually a form of type 2 respiratory failure which is failed gas exchange. It occurs when the blood supplying the alveoli doesnt contain enough CO2.  D- Diffusion impairment is also a cause of type 2 respiratory failure. It occurs when the blood doesnt contain enough oxygen because it cannot diffuse through the membrane into the blood (usually occurs in severe hypoxia)  E- Hypoventilation is the cause of type 3 respiratory failure which is mixed respiratory failure. It causes a combination of the symptoms of both types 1 and 2. This usually occurs in obstructive sleep apnoea where the patient stops breathing briefly multiple times during sleep. Neurotransmitter release is an active process mediated by voltage gated calcium channels. Neurone stimulation causes an influx of Ca2+ through voltage gated ion channels in the presynaptic membrane which activates Ca2+ dependent proteins that induce vesicles containing neurotransmitters to fuse with the plasma membrane of the presynaptic neurone. Neurotransmitters are then released into the synaptic cleft where they bind to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. Receptors on the post-synaptic membrane are either ionotropic or metabotropic. Ionotropic receptors cause changes in permeability of the membrane to specific ions. Metabotropic receptors cause intracellular signalling cascades which result in changes to postsynaptic membrane polarity. Neurotransmitters are usually removed from the synapse by one of three methods; active uptake (eg. glutamate), enzymatic degradation or passive diffusion. Flat bones are typically found in areas of the body where extensive organ protection is required. For example- skull and sternum. They also provide levers for muscle attachment e.g. scapula and clavicle. Finally, they serve as sites for the production of blood cells e.g. sternum, ribs, pelvic girdle.  Long bones provide a lever for muscle attachment and provide strength and support for the body. For example- humerus, femur, tibia, fibula, patella, metacarpal, phalanges. Short bones are found in the hands and wrists. They are typically round or oval and provide weight bearing surfaces for the body (e.g. carpal and tarsal bones). Sesamoid bones are found close to tendons and act to reduce friction between the two surfaces. An example of this is the kneecap. Sutural bones are very small and flat, forming the joints between bones of the cranium. They may be fused to adjacent bones or present independently. Examples include the bones of the ethmoid plate and sphenoid bone.
